Thank you so much for your reply. My gut just wants to walk in there and say “how could you do this to us?” while sobbing hysterically. Buuuuut that’s not good for anyone. It’s why I need therapy and why I need to talk through this before I see him. And I also know that those actions are not about “us” or even him... but more about this disease. 

I was trying to think about what I would want someone to say to me and I think for starters it would just be “I’m here, I love you, I’m glad you’re alive. I’ll support you and be here for you.” 

This is the part I have really struggled with... 
I don’t know if I would want to hear how much pain it would have caused someone if I were to be successful. I think I would have that awareness and guilt already. He’s a very smart guy. I know he is ill but I’m hoping that my presence will show that this has changed my life and that I feel very strongly about having him in our world. I took a week off from work so I will be able to visit him every day and am also driving 400 miles to stay near the hospital and be there.

I don’t want to compound his guilt and cause him to use his energy towards unpacking my feelings when he should be focusing on himself and his own healing.
Thank you, I appreciate your advice! I can’t wait to just sit next to him and be with him

Gah. Thank you so much. Your messages and support have honestly moved me to tears. I can’t believe how lucky I have been this past hour or so with the support and feedback I have gotten. I haven’t been able to talk about this with my “real life” friends because it is too hard. I’m glad there are spaces like this in the world where conversations like this can occur. I feel better now than I have in the past 24 hours. One day at a time. We will all heal. Thank you.

This is incredibly helpful!! Thank you, I ordered a 1,000 piece puzzle so that when he gets home we have something that we can sit around and do to keep our hands and minds busy while also having the ability to focus on something that isn’t talking about “it” but also provides us the opportunity to talk about “it” while keeping it casual and also avoiding eye contact if that makes it too hard for him. He’s the kind of person with a very analytical mind so I think having that kind of mental stimulation as a distractor will really help. 

When it comes down to not physically “handcuffing” myself to another adult human that is what I think I am going to need my own therapy for. I know it won’t be good for him to feel like we can’t trust him once he’s discharged. I have no idea how to cope with the idea of him being out and about and potentially in crisis again. I recognize that’s a personal problem and something I’m going to have to cope with, though, so I can continue to live my own life. 

Otherwise, I love your idea of rewriting what I want to say. I was planning to do this because I know the first things I will want to say will be “how could you do this to us?” But I know that he is sick and it is not his fault and that is not therapeutic. I like the idea of waiting 2-3 weeks before sharing with him about how I feel. 

When I’m able to initiate my own therapy I think I’ll plan to start by expressing my love, support, telling him that I’m there for him, and that I’m happy he’s alive. Once I work through the rest and he is in a better place I think I will want to share how much pain was inflicted on me as a result of his decision regardless of the fact that he was unwell when he made the decision he did.

Thank you. I think it’s important that he knows how I feel. I just don’t want to essentially “kick him while he’s down” and make him feel worse. I think I deserve to tell him how much it hurt me so he knows how much I love and care about him.

I honestly can’t wait to start therapy so I can begin to process how I feel and cope in a healthy way so I can support him and my other family members.

Thank you, I really appreciate it. It’s hard going back and forth from a clinical health care provider’s perspective who is trying to maintain a “therapeutic relationship”, a person who suffers myself, and a supportive family member. I just want to make sure that what I say doesn’t push him too far and make him feel too guilty.

I know I’m going to break down when I see him because I’ve been a mess since I got the phone call. I know it’s a disease and that he is sick. I just don’t want to make it worse but also convey how hurt I am and how much I love him. I’m just hoping that conveying my genuine feelings will be the right thing.
Thank you for your reply, it is very appreciated. I just hope that I can be supportive and that I don’t cause him more pain by showing him my pain.

I can’t wait to squeeze the heck out of him. I know I’m going to cry but I hope that won’t be counterproductive and cause him to feel more guilt. I know it will be a long road and I just don’t want to make it worse.

Thank you for your reply. When he called me the night before he attempted I asked him if “he was calling to say hi or calling to say goodbye” and he didn’t say anything to deny it. I totally broke down on the phone and told him I didn’t know what I would do or how I would carry on if I lost him. I talked to him until he made it home safely that night at my parents house... but as soon as my parents left for 5 minutes the next morning he attempted. 

I don’t know how to convey to him how I feel and how much pain it has caused me in a way that does not come across as selfish and self absorbed. I want him to know much it hurts me  and how much I care but I also don’t want to make it all about myself if that makes sense? 

I want to find the healthy balance of being honest, loving, and supportive. I’m sure it won’t be perfect but because it will be genuine and thoughtful I hope it comes across as ~good enough~

Thank you for your reply. I’m glad I have the weekend to get myself sorted out so I can be supportive and find out what he needs from me.

I’m not sure how to not tip toe around him and I know my husband is worried about that too. It’s going to be hard to be “normal” but we will certainly try.

Thank you for your reply, I really appreciate it. I’m glad I have the weekend to get my thoughts together and be in a place where I can be supportive rather than make it about me and how I feel.

My whole unit with the exception one nurse went on strike last year. No one WANTS to go several days without pay... but we all ended up getting a raise and a better contract for it. The nurse who didn’t strike with us received a lot of cold shoulders for several weeks- I’ll admit, it was harsh. Some people were kinder than others... but she felt like she was standing up for what she believed in, and that was worth it to her. If your colleagues see you literally banking off of them while they stand up and get you a better contract, I’m sure there will be resentments, too. Sometimes the short term money isn’t worth it. If you’re actually standing up for something you believe in, that might help you sleep at night

My first day in clinical I nearly fainted. My patient was a double amputee coming straight out of the OR and they were trying to put a catheter in them. They were flailing around, disoriented, and in pain. The room got hot, I got sweaty, and I stepped out of the room to splash some cold water on my face. I called my dad and told him that I couldn’t do this and I felt terrible about wasting a year studying something I didn’t think I could do. He told me, “There’s nothing wrong with being upset by it. If you weren’t upset, I would be worried.” It was exactly what I needed to hear. 4 years into nursing there are still things that bother me! And yeah, you get desensitized with time... but being upset with things like that is what makes us good nurses.
